---
title: "Assessment planning: G-study and D-study report"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
params:
  ratings_csv: null
  output_dir: "gtheory-report-files"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(mfrmr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5)
example_run <- is.null(params$ratings_csv)
if (example_run) {
  data("mfrmr_example_gtheory_crossed", package = "mfrmr")
  ratings <- mfrmr_example_gtheory_crossed
} else {
  ratings <- read.csv(params$ratings_csv, check.names = FALSE)
}
# Edit these choices before examining results. No automatic weight selection.
scores <- c("Content", "Organization")
weights <- c(Content = .5, Organization = .5)
plans <- expand.grid(Raters = c(2, 4), Tasks = c(3, 6))
g <- mfrm_g_study(ratings, scores = scores, person = "Person",
  rater = "Rater", task = "Task")
d <- mfrm_d_study(g, plans, weights = weights)
component_ci <- confint(g, weights = weights, assumption = "normal")
intervals <- setNames(lapply(c("G", "Phi", "RelativeSEM", "AbsoluteSEM"),
  function(metric) confint(d, parm = metric, composite = "Composite",
    assumption = "normal", method = if (metric %in% c("G", "Phi")) "delta" else "auto")),
  c("G", "Phi", "RelativeSEM", "AbsoluteSEM"))
comparison <- mfrm_multivariate_d_compare(d, reference = 1,
  composite = "Composite", assumption = "normal")
study_context <- c(
  question = "Compare prespecified rater/task counts for the fixed Content-Organization composite",
  rating_unit = "One Person by Rater by Task row with two fixed score components",
  score_direction = "Specify separately what higher Content and Organization values mean",
  transformation = "Raw numeric components; no normalization; supplied composite weights"
)
g_report <- mfrm_report(g, intervals = component_ci, style = "apa", study_context = study_context)
report <- mfrm_report(d, intervals = intervals, style = "apa", study_context = study_context)
comparison_report <- mfrm_report(comparison, style = "apa", study_context = study_context)
composite <- d$coefficients[d$coefficients$Kind == "Composite", ]
out <- params$output_dir
dir.create(out, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## Relate this report to the assessment question

When combining measurement and G/D studies, report each analysis's input unit,
retained sample, score scale, facets, aggregation, weights and uncertainty
separately. Explain what MFRM reveals about specific facet effects and what
G/D reveals about reproducibility of the defined observed score and future
plans. Do not treat Rasch-adjusted estimates as interchangeable with raw G-study
scores. The package's `mfrmr-networks-and-reporting` vignette shows published
speaking/writing examples and a FACETS/ConQuest reporting crosswalk. Select
linking, bias and model-comparison modules from `mfrmr-reporting-and-apa` when
they address the question; this template does not run every possible analysis.

## Question and score meaning

`r if (example_run) "**Synthetic teaching example:** these are continuous scores generated from independent normal random effects, not empirical speaking-assessment findings." else "**Study draft:** complete the context and interpretation below before manuscript use."`

Would adding raters or tasks improve the dependability and precision of a
prespecified Content–Organization composite? This report connects the source
of error to the practical choice of rating plan. Its tables include both
relative ranking and absolute-score decisions; emphasize the target actually
used in your study.

**Complete for your study:** define participants and recruitment, the assessment
purpose, rater/task populations and sampling, assignment, training and missing
ratings. Give each score's units, endpoint labels, coding and direction.
For Comprehensibility, explicitly state whether higher means easier or harder
to understand. Explain any reversal before defining the composite. G theory
does not establish that ordinal categories are an interval scale.

The present template treats Content and Organization as **fixed score
components**, with weights `r paste(names(weights), weights, sep = " = ", collapse = ", ")`.
They are not random criteria or separate latent abilities. Weights are used
as supplied; adapt this template's prose as well as its code if that target
changes.

## Source design and estimation

A complete crossed Person × Rater × Task G-study was estimated by balanced
multivariate ANOVA. Persons are the differentiation target. Raters and tasks
are random sampling facets; the numeric score columns are fixed components.
Each source has a variance–covariance matrix across those scores. The
composite's source variance is the quadratic form of that matrix and the
fixed weights. The default raw-component policy preserves signed estimates.

```{r design}
knitr::kable(report$tables$source_counts, caption = "Observed source levels")
knitr::kable(report$tables$source_rows, caption = "Source row accounting")
knitr::kable(report$tables$component_diagnostics, digits = 4,
  caption = "Component admissibility; inspect before interpreting projections")
```

If your design is incomplete or nested, change the G-study specification,
interval methods and this Methods section together. Do not fill missing
ratings with zero or count unassigned ratings as missing scores. One
observation per Person–Rater–Task cell means the residual combines the
three-way interaction and within-cell error. A random-facet interpretation
requires a defensible sampling universe; the software does not establish it.

## Which sources contribute variation?

```{r components}
knitr::kable(g_report$tables$intervals[, c("Source", "Estimate", "SE", "Lower", "Upper", "Status")],
  digits = 3, caption = "Composite source variances and component intervals")
component_plot <- plot(g, weights = weights)
```

The figure shows the original composite component estimates. Variances have
squared score units. The table adds approximate normal-model component
intervals (with the residual's chi-square reference); signed points and
unavailable intervals remain visible. Component SE is sampling uncertainty
in a variance, distinct from measurement SEM. Cross-score covariances and
all source matrices are retained in the exported report.

## Compare the prespecified future plans

Future counts describe complete balanced ratings from the same populations,
assuming invariant source components. Larger future counts do not enlarge
the source sample or make its estimates more certain.

```{r plans}
knitr::kable(composite[, c("Scenario", "Raters", "Tasks", "UniverseVariance",
  "RelativeErrorVariance", "AbsoluteErrorVariance", "G", "Phi", "RelativeSEM", "AbsoluteSEM", "Status")],
  digits = 3, caption = "Composite dependability, error variances and measurement SEM")
planning_plot <- plot(d, composite = "Composite", metric = "G", x_var = "Tasks",
  panel_by = "Raters", intervals = intervals$G)
sem_plot <- plot(d, type = "sem", composite = "Composite", metric = "AbsoluteSEM",
  x_var = "Tasks", panel_by = "Raters", intervals = intervals$AbsoluteSEM)
```

G describes relative decisions, whereas Phi includes sources relevant to
absolute decisions. Neither is inter-rater agreement. Both depend on the
Person universe variance as well as error; report SEM and error variances
alongside the coefficients (Brennan, 2003). SEM is expressed in the composite's
score units, not logits or a Person posterior SD.

```{r uncertainty}
knitr::kable(report$tables$intervals[, c("Scenario", "Metric", "Estimate", "Lower", "Upper", "Level", "Method", "Status")],
  digits = 3, caption = "Prespecified composite targets: uncertainty and availability")
```

The coefficient intervals here explicitly use the normal-theory delta
approximation; SEM uses the recorded MLS/chi-square rule. These are
method-specific, pointwise intervals under independent normal random effects.
They are not distribution-robust, simultaneous or adjusted for selecting a
plan. Jiang et al. (2022) motivate attention to coefficient uncertainty,
especially in small designs; that study does not establish coverage for all
methods used here. Keep any unavailable result and its reason.

## Paired comparison and practical answer

```{r paired}
knitr::kable(comparison$comparisons[, c("Reference", "Scenario", "Metric",
  "Difference", "SE", "Lower", "Upper", "Status")], digits = 3,
  caption = "Plan minus reference plan: shared-source normal-theory delta approximation")
```

All plans use the same estimated source, so these comparisons retain their
shared sampling covariance. Positive coefficient differences and negative
SEM differences favor the comparison plan on those metrics. The calculation
does not rank costs or guarantee classification accuracy at a cut score.

**Complete the answer:** "For [score and population], changing [raters/tasks]
from [reference] to [plan] changed projected [metric] by [estimate], with
[method and level] interval [limits]. Relative to [practical precision target],
this [supports/does not resolve] the change because [magnitude, uncertainty,
cost and burden]." State the time/cost per task and per rating, feasibility,
and consequences of errors. Use a threshold chosen for the intended decision,
not a universal coefficient cutoff or the best-looking plan.

## Saved evidence and references

```{r exports, include=FALSE}
export_summary_appendix(g_report, output_dir = out, prefix = "gstudy", overwrite = TRUE)
export_summary_appendix(report, output_dir = out, prefix = "dstudy", overwrite = TRUE)
export_summary_appendix(comparison_report, output_dir = out, prefix = "comparison", overwrite = TRUE)
figures <- list(components = component_plot, planning = planning_plot, sem = sem_plot)
for (name in names(figures)) {
  ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, paste0(name, ".png")),
    as_ggplot(figures[[name]]), width = 7.5, height = 5, dpi = 180)
}
saveRDS(list(g = g, d = d, component_intervals = component_ci, intervals = intervals,
  comparison = comparison, reports = list(g = g_report, d = report, comparison = comparison_report),
  figures = figures, session = sessionInfo()), file.path(out, "gtheory-analysis.rds"))
```

The `r out` directory contains full CSV/HTML tables, figure PNGs and the
reloadable analysis, including weights, source/plan context, method notes and
unavailable states. Source archives may include participant identifiers;
review them before sharing. Rendering this editable template reruns its
analysis; reopening the saved reports or plots does not refit it.

- Brennan, R. L. (2003). *Coefficients and indices in generalizability theory*.
  CASMA Research Report No. 1, University of Iowa.
- Jiang, Z., Raymond, M., DiStefano, C., Shi, D., Liu, R., & Sun, J. (2022).
  A Monte Carlo study of confidence interval methods for generalizability
  coefficient. *Educational and Psychological Measurement, 82*, 705–718.
  [doi:10.1177/00131644211033899](https://doi.org/10.1177/00131644211033899).
